newsitem.title: UK: Hong Kong bourse chief sees growth after handover.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong bourse chief sees growth after handover.

text.p: The ambitious Hong Kong stock market is poised to become the premier exchange in Asia, eventually pushing Tokyo bourse to second place, according to the head of the Hong Kong Stock Exchange (HKSE).
"I see Hong Kong becoming the London of Asia and the Manhattan of China but it will take time. Over the next 10 years we will eventually grow into that," HKSE chairman Dr Edgar Wai-Kim Cheng said.
Cheng said international investors had nothing to fear when China takes over the British colony in nine weeks' time. Indeed, the mainland's economic might would act as a catalyst toward growth.
"There will be a lot of pleasant surprises rather than the doom and gloom stories that have been talked about," Cheng told Reuters in an interview.
"Given the chance, the new government will be able to show that a lot of concerns are not well founded."
Cheng, in London to address a conference on the globalisation of the securities markets, is confident the HKSE will be allowed to conduct its business without interference from Beijing.
He said that the freedoms enjoyed under British rule had been "enshrined" in the Sino-British Joint Declaration agreement.

The declaration, signed in December 1984 by then Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher and the Chinese government, promises Hong Kong will keep its capitalist lifestyle and a high degree of autonomy until 2047.
Confidence in that pledge was dented in June 1989 when Chinese tanks crushed a democracy movement in Beijing with heavy loss of life but Cheng is not expecting any crackdown on its market freedoms.
"It is written into the law -- one country, two systems. We will retain our own systems and I don't see why that will change in the future."
However, Cheng is anticipating big changes over the next 10 years in the number of major Chinese companies or "red chips" that will list in Hong Kong.
"I'm very optimistic about Chinese companies coming to Hong Kong to get listed. But they have to abide by our listing rules and regulations," Cheng said.
He noted that over the past three years 26 Chinese companies had listed in Hong Kong, raising around $4.5 billion but representing less than one percent of the bourse's total market capitalisation.

The ending of 150 years of British rule of the "Fragrant Harbour", the Chinese meaning of Hong Kong, should lead to more red chip listings as both countries become more familiar with each other, Cheng said.

"Both Hong Kong and China have been very careful about bringing Chinese enterprises to Hong Kong. We have been trying to understand the systems in China and China has been trying to understand Hong Kong systems.

This dialogue over the past few years has resulted in China accepting, amongst other things, that international securities investors require transparency in share transactions and timely corporate information.
"Issues such as timely disclosures have improved. Things like the annual reports are now as of good as standard as anywhere else," Cheng said.
He thinks Hong Kong will eventually surpass the Tokyo bourse, currently in the process of deregulating its "restrictive" market.

Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto unveiled plans in November to liberalise Japan's financial markets under "Big Bang" reforms in which banks, brokers, and insurance companies will be allowed to enter each other's turf.
But these reforms are not due to be in place until the year 2001 by which time, Hong Kong could take centre stage in Asia, Cheng said.
"What makes Hong Kong tick is our market's openness. We have very little if any government intervention," Cheng said.
"We do have a regulatory body but the exchange is market driven rather than government limitation and I believe after July 1, 1997, that will not change."
